That is roughly 240 weeks with zero qualifying agreements — a per-week base rate near 1–2%. A six-day window therefore starts very low, though it rises sharply if talks are in an endgame.

Strongest evidence for "Yes": If, as of late October 2026, negotiations have advanced to leader-level summits with leaked draft texts, both sides face mounting costs (manpower, economics, US pressure), and either side has signaled a date-certain deal, the conditional chance of a signed suspension within days becomes plausible.

Strongest evidence for "No": The track record — every prior deadline and framework has collapsed over territory, security guarantees, sanctions relief, and sequencing. Both sides have incentives to keep fighting for leverage, and Russia in particular has historically slow-walked agreements.

What it turns on: Whether a mutually announced suspension with a specified effective date occurs before 11:59 PM ET on October 31. Watch for a summit announcement or joint statement; unilateral pauses or "frameworks without effective dates" do not qualify.
